title: 夫と娘を残して初めての国外出張　夫の試練と私の気づき
extracted_text: ベルリン支局・五十嵐朋子記者が車いすユーザーの夫との暮らしを通じ、ドイツと日本の違いや「共生」について考えます。 車いすユーザーの夫、諏訪正晃（40）は3月15日、私（記者、40歳）のいなくなった自宅の居間で、開けっぱなしになった窓を恨めしそうに見上げていた。私がハンガリー総選挙（4月12日）の事前取材のために出張に行ったため、夫は1歳の娘の面倒を5日間1人でみることになった。試練とも言える娘との二人っきりの日々をいかに乗り切ったのだろうか。 赴任して2年、これまで国内出張の経験はあったが、国外出張、それも3泊以上の出張は初めてだった。私がベルリンをたったのは3月14日。出張への緊張はもちろんあったが、正直に言えば、夫と娘を2人きりで残す不安のほうが勝った。 翌15日に早速トラブルが起きていた。私が居間の窓を開けっぱなしにしたまま出張に行ったせいで、室内は冷え込んだ。この日のベルリンの最高気温は7・2度。窓を閉めようにも、高い位置にある窓の開閉ハンドルには、車椅子からでは手が届かない。 幸い、日曜日で保育園のないこの日だけは、夫が息抜きできるようベビーシッターを頼んでいた。ちょうど居合わせたベビーシッターが一緒にガラスを片付けてくれて、窓も閉めてくれた。 起床して元気に走り回る娘を捕まえて着替えさせ、膝に乗せて腹巻きで体同士を固定する。いつもの登園スタイルで車椅子で一緒に保育園に向かう。 「元気？　今日もかわいいわね」。たまにすれ違う、名前も知らない近所の初老の女性とあいさつした。娘も最近覚えた「チュー（さようなら）」を言いながら手を振る。気さくでゆるやかな交流があるのはベルリンのいいところで、「何かあっても誰かが助けてくれる」と安心感をもたらしてくれた。
translated_text: Berlin Bureau reporter Tomoko Igarashi reflects on differences between Germany and Japan and about "coexistence" through her life with her wheelchair-using husband. Her wheelchair-using husband, Masaaki Suwa (40), was on March 15th, looking up resentfully at the window left open in the living room of their home where she (the reporter, 40) was absent. Because she went on a business trip for pre-coverage of the Hungarian general election (April 12th), her husband had to take care of their 1-year-old daughter alone for 5 days. How did they survive those days alone together, which could be called a trial? It has been two years since I was posted here. I had domestic business trip experience before, but this was my first overseas business trip, and also my first trip lasting three nights or more. I left for Berlin on March 14th. Of course I was nervous about the trip, but honestly, the anxiety about leaving husband and daughter alone was greater. The next day, on the 15th, trouble arose right away. Because I left the living room window open when I departed for the trip, the room had grown cold. The high temperature in Berlin that day was 7.2 degrees. Even if I wanted to close the window, the handle for opening and closing it is located too high to reach from a wheelchair. Luckily, because it was Sunday and there was no daycare, the husband had called a babysitter so he could get a break. The babysitter who happened to be there helped clear the broken glass and closed the window. I caught my daughter as she woke up and ran around energetically, got her dressed, and held her on my lap, securing our bodies together with a belly wrap. We headed to daycare together in the wheelchair using the usual routine. "Are you feeling well? You look cute today." I greeted an older woman from the neighborhood whom I sometimes pass by but don't know by name. My daughter waved her hand while saying "choo" (goodbye), which she recently learned. The easygoing and relaxed interactions are one of the good things about Berlin, and give me a sense of security that "someone will help if anything happens."
title_en: First Overseas Trip Leaving Husband and Daughter: My Husband's Ordeal and My Realization
